rationale: Leek-like leaves, smooth stem and acorn-shaped root tubers fit a large tuberous asphodel (A. ramosus/aestivus group). A. fistulosus has a hollow stem and fibrous roots.
Spiny trailing shrub, hooked thorns, round leaves, pickled buds and an olive-like fruit opening to a white flower: the caper.
Partitioned poppy-like capsule with black pungent aromatic seed sprinkled on bread is the black cumin. The culinary use points to the cultivated N. sativa.
Coriander-like leaflets on very black, thin stalks, no flower or fruit, near springs and on wet walls: maidenhair fern.
Thick squill-like leaves with sparse marginal spines and a bitter juice describe medicinal aloe. Growth on Andros and Asian coasts fits A. vera; the imported Indian drug could include other species.
White stem, abrotanum-like narrow leaves and golden dry corymbs used for crowning images and against moths fit an everlasting Helichrysum. H. stoechas is the usual identification.
Large white-spotted leaves and an erect two-cubit stem, mottled purple and snake-like, are diagnostic of the dragon arum.
A smaller unspotted dracontium-like aroid with an edible, less acrid white root is an Arum. The Syrian name loupha suggests a Levantine Arum that may not be listed.
Ivy-like leaves mottled whitish, a leafless short scape with rose-purple flowers and a flattened turnip-like tuber: a Cyclamen. Ivy-shaped leaves favour C. hederifolium.
Vine-like cut leaves, chickpea-like pods and rough triangular acrid seeds used as an emetic and against lice: stavesacre.
A wild grapevine with small black astringent grapes and powers like the cultivated vine is wild Vitis vinifera (subsp. sylvestris).
A sweet, boxwood-yellow root from Cappadocia and Pontus is liquorice. Rough plane-ball-like fruit heads lean towards G. echinata, but the drug root is usually G. glabra.
The chapter describes three henbanes; the black, purple-flowered, spiny-capsuled kind is H. niger. The preferred white kind is H. albus, so niger is only part of the description.
Of the three henbanes, the purple-flowered black kind is H. niger and the quince-yellow-flowered kind with yellowish seed may be H. aureus.
The recommended white-flowered, white-seeded, soft downy henbane of seashores and ruins is H. albus. The black kind is H. niger.
Ivy-like but softer, rounder leaves, a purple flower at the root like a henbane capsule, and aromatic jointed rhizomes from shady mountains: asarabacca.
Hollow jointed stems with rush-like whorls in wet ditches suggest horsetail (Equisetum). The climbing habit and the synonyms anabasion/ephedron suggest a climbing Ephedra mixed in.
Small flower heads with a golden disc and white, yellow or purple rays and an apple-like smell describe chamomile-type composites. Three kinds are treated, so a single species is uncertain.
Hairy weed with a leafy stem, heads clustered at the top and black flea-like seeds is fleawort. P. afra and P. arenaria are the classic sources of the seed.
Two plantains: the greater, broad-leaved and growing in wet places, is P. major. The smaller, narrow-leaved one is likely P. lanceolata or P. lagopus.
The greater plantain, broad-leaved and growing in moist places, is best matched by P. major. P. asiatica is outside the region.
The great centaury has walnut-like serrate leaves, poppy-like heads with blue flowers and a thick red-juiced root: a Centaurea-type composite, not the small gentianaceous centaury.
Large serrate leaves, knapweed-like heads with bluish flowers, cnicus-like fruit and a massive red-juiced root from Lycia and Arcadia fit Rhaponticoides (Centaurea) centaurium.
Leek-like leaves, a triangular rush-like stem and fragrant black olive-shaped or round tubers from marshy ground describe sedge (Cyperus). Both oblong and round tubers are mentioned.
The Roman vettonica with a square stem, oak-like crenate leaves and a spike like thymbra is betony, usually Betonica officinalis, which is not listed. B. alopecuros is a congeneric alternative.
Single stiff hairy stem, pinnately cut serrate leaves and downward-bent hooked fruits that cling to clothing: agrimony.
A familiar shrub with long almond-like leaves, rose-like flowers and horn-shaped pods full of plumed seed, toxic to animals: oleander.
Leaves like a centipede, cut like polypody, yellowish and scaly beneath, growing on shaded rocks and walls, used for the spleen: rustyback fern.
Edible garden strychnos: a small branched herb with dark basil-like leaves and round green or black berries, harmless to eat and cooling. This is black nightshade.
A tree with olive-like leaves, white fragrant clustered flowers, from Ascalon and Canopus, whose leaves dye hair: henna.

Stemless rosettes with apple-like fragrant fruits and forked roots, anaesthetic before surgery: mandrake. The female and male kinds fall within Mandragora; the shady-cave morion is sometimes read as Atropa.

Stemless rosettes with apple-like fragrant fruits and forked roots, anaesthetic before surgery: mandrake. The female and male kinds fall within Mandragora; the shady-cave morion is sometimes read as Atropa.
A span-high fern on mossy rocks and oak stumps with a hairy, tentacled, sweetish rhizome used as a purgative: polypody.
A tall hollow-stemmed white-leaved thistle with an urchin-like oblong spiny head and purple flowers fits a large cardoon-like thistle (Onopordum/Notobasis type). The identity is not secure.
Three birthworts; the round female kind with a turnip-like tuber is A. rotunda. The long kind and klematitis are other species.
The long and klematitis birthworts have slender stems and long roots. A. longa/clematitis-type plants are the usual readings, and the listed species only partly cover them.
The Cretan daukos, with fennel-like fine leaves, white hairy aromatic fruit, on sunny rocks, is the classic Athamanta cretensis. The other two kinds are less certain umbellifers.
A wild staphylinos with a dill-like umbel of white flowers and a small purple floret in the centre is the wild carrot.
Plantain-like basal leaves, a hollow jointed two-cubit stem and a long thick bitter root from high shady wet mountains (Illyria): great yellow gentian.
Saffron-coloured acrid latex, glaucous buttercup-like leaves and a long slender poppy-like pod: greater celandine. Lesser celandine is the separate small chelidonion.
A tall jointed fennel-like stem, heavy-smelling ferula-like leaves, white umbels and a lethal chilling action: poison hemlock.
White woolly cabbage-like leaves and a tall stem describe mulleins (Verbascum); several kinds are listed. The wild sage-leaved kind with golden whorls is Phlomis fruticosa.
A white hairy square-stemmed bush with round wrinkled bitter leaves and whorled rough flowers, near ruins, used for coughs: white horehound.
A spiny hedge shrub with oblong soft leaves (Lycium/Rhamnus type). The third kind's flat winged fruit points to Paliurus, which is not listed.
Hairy basil-like leaves and a white-purplish inflorescence coiled like a scorpion's tail: heliotrope.
A trifoliate shrubby legume smelling of rue when young and of bitumen when grown, with purple flowers and beaked pods: pitch trefoil.
A rough single-stemmed undershrub with round leaves and double shield-like fruits fits a crucifer with clypeate silicles (Fibigia/Alyssum). The identity is not secure.

The black vine (bryonia), ivy/smilax-like leaves, climbing with tendrils, edible young shoots and a root black outside and boxwood-yellow within: traditionally black bryony (Tamus). Black berries also fit Bryonia alba.
Sword-like leaves, multicoloured nodding flowers and jointed fragrant rhizomes from Illyria and Macedonia, dried for orris: a bearded iris of the germanica/florentina/pallida group.
A span-high hairy umbellifer with fine fennel-like leaves and a white fragrant umbel, eaten as a pot-herb. The description is too brief to fix the genus.
Sticky hairy olive-like leaves, yellow pappose flower heads and use against fleas and gnats describe fleabane. The larger is D. viscosa and the smaller, more fragrant one is D. graveolens.
The larger heavy-smelling konyza with sticky olive-like leaves fits D. viscosa. The chapter also covers a smaller and a third kind.
Myrtle-like but sharp-pointed cladodes with a red berry borne in the middle of the 'leaf', and asparagus-like edible shoots: butcher's broom.
A thin smooth stem with laurel-like leaves bearing red round fruits on the leaves points to a Ruscus/Danae-type plant, R. hypophyllum being the closest.
A creeping, curved, hairy herb smelling of pine, with yellow flowers: ground-pine (Ajuga chamaepitys). Two further kinds are described.
The pine-scented creeping herb with yellow flowers is A. chamaepitys. The second and third kinds may be other Ajuga or Teucrium species.
The pine-scented creeping herb with yellow flowers is A. chamaepitys. The third 'male' kind with white hairy leaves may be Ajuga iva or a Teucrium.
The tanner's sumac, used for curing hides and as a culinary spice, with serrate reddish leaves and dense clustered fruit: Rhus coriaria.
A square-stemmed labiate with horehound-like rough leaves and whorls with black seed, used for wounds, fits a Sideritis. The species is indeterminable from the text.
A low cushion with a woody root, small leaflets and hidden white stiff spines that yields gum tragacanth: a spiny Astragalus. The true gum sources (A. gummifer group) are not all listed.
The terrestrial tribolos, with purslane-like leaves and prostrate spiny stems, is Tribulus terrestris. The aquatic one with an edible starchy nut eaten by the Thracians is Trapa natans.
